summary.text: Oxygen dissolves into seawater at the surface, both by mixing with the air and through photosynthesis by phytoplankton.
Less oxygen can dissolve as water gets warmer and saltier, and warm surface water also mixes less with the oxygen-poorer water below.
The oceans have lost 1-2% of their oxygen since the mid-20th century, a threat to sea life and to people who depend on it.

facts.label: Oxygen sources
facts.value: Mixing with air and phytoplankton photosynthesis

facts.label: Projected decline
facts.value: Up to 7% over the next hundred years

facts.label: Warming's share
facts.value: About half of upper-ocean oxygen loss

items.prompt: Two patches of sea are alike except that one is several degrees warmer. Which can hold more dissolved oxygen?
items.explain: Oxygen's solubility drops as water warms, so cooler water can hold more of it.

items.prompt: As the sea surface warms, less oxygen reaches deeper water. Why?

options.label: Warm water is buoyant, so it mixes less with deeper water
Warm water pushes its oxygen straight to the bottom
Fish crowd into warm water and use up all the oxygen
Heat breaks oxygen molecules apart in the water

items.explain: Warmer water is more buoyant, so layers mix less and less oxygen-rich surface water reaches the deeper ocean.

items.prompt: Years of farm and sewage pollution flow into a bay until the oxygen in its water falls to very low levels. What are such places commonly called?
items.explain: Coastal oxygen loss driven by nutrient pollution is known as dead zones.

items.prompt: Oxygen enters the open ocean at the top, but living things use it at every depth. Where do naturally oxygen-poor layers usually sit?
items.explain: Oxygen minimum zones generally occur at middle depths, roughly 100 to 1000 m down.

items.prompt: What naturally creates the open ocean's low-oxygen zones in the first place?

options.label: Too little sunlight reaching the seabed
Respiration of organic matter sinking from above
Salt crystals blocking oxygen from dissolving

items.explain: These zones result from the respiration of organic material that is produced near the surface and sinks.

items.prompt: Since the middle of the 20th century, roughly how much of their oxygen have the world's oceans lost?
items.explain: Studies show the oceans have already lost 1-2% of their oxygen, with up to 7% more loss projected over the next century.
